utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good afternoon to everybody. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-14-A, the Prosecution versus Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can everyone hear me? Interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Can the appellant hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question, Your Honour. I don't believe he heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I repeat: Can the appellant hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I hear you well, and I can understand everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. The Defence can hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We can, Your Honour. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to call for appearances of the parties. I turn first to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Appearing for the appellant is Russell Hayman, with my colleagues, to my left, Anto Nobilo, Andrew Paley, and Robert Perrin. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Appearing for the Prosecution on the evidentiary hearing will be Norman Farrell, Mr. Andrew Cayley, and Ms. Susan Grogan as our case manager. During the course of the hearing, as you know, there is going to be seven witnesses called and there are other counsel who are involved in other matters who have agreed to assist in the evidentiary hearing, and that will be Mr. Mark Harmon and Mr. Ken Scott, and they will appear at the time when necessary for the purpose of raising questions with the witnesses, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. I would like now to make a few brief introductory remarks before we proceed with the evidentiary phase of this hearing. As announced by the registrar, the case before us today is the Prosecutor versus Tihomir Blaskic. General Blaskic was indicted for persecutions, unlawful attacks on civilians and civilian objects, wilful killing and causing serious injury, destruction and plunder of property, destruction of institutions dedicated to religion or education, and inhumane treatment, the taking of hostages and the use of human shields. The indictment contained 20 counts, each of which alleged the responsibility under both Article 7(1) and 7(3) of the Tribunal's Statute. The counts concerned violation of Articles 2, 3, and 5 of the Statute, allegedly committed in the period from May 1992 to January 1994, in Central Bosnia. From 27 June 1992, Mr. Blaskic was the commander of the Croatian Defence Council, known as the HVO, armed forces in Central Bosnia. The judgement in this case was rendered on the 3rd of March, 2000. The Trial Chamber convicted Mr. Blaskic of persecutions, murder, and inhumane acts, as crimes against humanity, as well as violations of Articles 2 and 3 of the Statute. Mr. Blaskic filed his notice of appeal on 17 of March, 2000. The Prosecution did not appeal. During the appellate proceedings, the appellant filed four motions pursuant to Rule 115 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, seeking to admit over 8.000 pages of material as additional evidence on appeal. The first of this additional evidence motions was filed on 19 January 2001, and the last on 12 May 2003. On the 31st of October, 2002, the Appeal Chamber issued a Scheduling Order in relation to the first three Rule 115 motions that had been filed by the appellant by that time. It deemed clearly admissible certain of the additional evidence sought to be admitted by the appellant and ordered the parties to present oral argument limited to the issue of whether the clearly admissible evidence justified a new trial by a Trial Chamber on some or all of the counts. On 21st November 2002, oral arguments were heard pursuant to this order. On 22nd November, 2002, a Scheduling Order was issued by the Appeals Chamber, allowing the Prosecution to file its rebuttal material. Following the filing of the fourth and final Rule 115 motion by the appellant and rebuttal material by the Prosecution in relation to this motion, the Appeals Chamber rendered its decision on evidence on the 31st of October, 2003. It found that in the circumstances of this case, a retrial was not warranted. It decided which items of additional evidence and rebuttal material are admitted into the record. A total of 108 items have been admitted. Six of the admitted items from the second Rule 115 motion are transcripts of witness testimony heard in another case before this Tribunal. These witnesses will be heard in the evidentiary portion of this hearing as Defence witnesses. Also on 31st of October, 2003, another Scheduling Order was issued, setting today as the start date for the hearing on appeal, and allowing the parties to file supplementary briefs. A further Scheduling Order was issued on 2nd December 2003. As set out in that Scheduling Order, we are scheduled to start today and to adjourn at 7.00 p.m. this evening. The Defence will have one hour to conduct its direct examination of each witness. The Prosecution will then have 40 minutes to conduct its cross-examination, and the scope of this examination must be limited, as I will set out later. The Defence will have 20 minutes for its re-examination. These times may be adjusted by the Chamber where appropriate. I would like to remind counsel for the Defence and the Prosecution that, of course, they are not obliged to use all the time allocated to them. As to the scope of the examination, the Chamber has issued this morning an order setting out the standard to be followed for the examination of witnesses on appeal. As indicated in this decision, the scope of the examination-in-chief of the witnesses may encompass any factual circumstance contained in the admitted evidence, as well as the alleged exculpatory evidence contained in the witness summaries disclosed by the Prosecution on 28th November 2003. After the questioning of the witness by the parties is completed, the Chamber may pose additional questions. I would like also to remind the parties that this is not a new trial. When an error of fact is alleged, the appellant must demonstrate that no reasonable trier of fact could have reached the conclusion being challenged and that this error has caused a miscarriage of justice. Of course, this demonstration has to take place in light also of the new evidence. Finally, the Prosecution is reminded that it is not allowed to contact the witnesses at any time during their testimony, and the appellant may contact them during the examination-in-chief, during the re-examination, and after cross-examination, but not during the cross-examination. Unless there are any questions, we will now proceed, but it is now necessary to go into closed session to hear the witnesses. The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: If I may, just before the witness enters. Just in terms of the scope, I just wanted to indicate to the Court the Prosecution's view of the scope of the first witness, based on the ruling. I've informed counsel for the Defence of the Prosecution's position in this regard, and I just wanted to put it on the record prior to the witness entering. Taking into consideration the guidelines that the Appeals Chamber has issued for the purposes of the examination this week, in relation to the first witness, there were six topics that were proposed by the appellant for the purposes of examination. I've reviewed the witness summaries and the proposed -- or the transcripts put forward by the appellant, and without, of course, limiting the scope of this examination in any way on the areas that have been admitted and which arise in the witness summaries, I just want to note for the record that the following four topics which are listed in the appellant's notice are not referred to by the witness anywhere, not in his two pages of transcripts that have been admitted, nor in his witness summaries in any respect. The first one is the nature and characteristics of certain military orders at issue. The second is the use and meaning of certain military terminology. The third is the existence of large amounts of explosives in Central Bosnia. And the fourth is the appellant's professional military character and lack of animus towards the Muslim population of Central Bosnia. Though, of course, the purpose of calling the witness, as I understand it, is to discuss the control over the military police and the special purpose units by Mr. Kordic, and the converse being the lack of control by Mr. Blaskic, the four topics that I have referred to are not found anywhere in the material before the Court. So the Prosecution fails to see how it could be something that would fall within the scope of the order, and I simply wanted to put that on the record before the witness arrived. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Yes, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will be going into all of these issues with at least some of the witnesses. We won't be going into each issue with every witness. For example, the first witness, we actually won't be going into each one of these issues, but it is our position that we could, under the scope of the examination order issued by the Court this morning, because all these issues are clearly implicated in the new evidence that has been admitted. So as I understand it, Mr. Farrell is making an objection for the record, but he would concede that these issues are implicated by the new evidence admitted as a result of the Rule 115 motions and therefore there isn't a need for argument on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I have to indicate that's not my position at all. There's no evidence upon which any of this is implicated. There's no evidence on the record of the four topics. They're not contained in the summaries and they're not contained in the two pages of transcripts. If my learned colleague would like to point me to those passages in which these arise, I'll be happy to reconsider my position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I can, Your Honour. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Hayman, you could do that pointing to passages when you put the questions later on, or you want to do it now? Because it may be a waste of time to do it now to engage in a discussion. When you put the specific question, we may address it --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm happy to do it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: -- more properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So can we now proceed to call the witness. But first we have to go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 9th day of December 2003, at 8.00 a.m. 23 24 25
